theses.title: The one-paragraph story
theses.text:
## The one-paragraph story

A predecessor system (not present in this repo) proved the concept and then
collapsed under its own success: roughly 140 accumulated feedback rules loaded
as prose pushed fresh sessions toward 400–500k tokens of always-on context,
where rules fired wrongly or vanished when needed most. In the project's RPG
vocabulary, it brought the **whole stash into every map** — as if a character
carried gear for every damage type when the encounter called only for cold
resistance. In plain language, irrelevant rules consumed attention and created
unintended interactions before the task began. The author's implementation
answers with _compiled_ rules: each correction becomes a typed mechanism (a
permission, a guard, a reactor, an evaluator, a transformer, a workflow gate)
attached only where relevant. A session in that profile gets **a build, not a
biography** — one active behavior, a handful of linked supports, its selected
safety layer, and the exact task state. The platform supplies the compiler and
mechanism contracts without prescribing that loadout. The [starter proof](../evidence/WO-118/README.md) completed resident-owned scratch delivery and review repair with writer replacement and resident restart; a fresh export demonstrated live status, while efficiency remains unmeasured.

theses.title: The core bet
theses.text:
## The core bet

> "The true work of the inventor consists in choosing among these combinations
> so as to eliminate the useless ones... the rules that must guide the choice
> are extremely fine and delicate. It's almost impossible to state them
> precisely; they must be felt rather than formulated." — Poincaré, via Pirsig

Generation is cheap and getting cheaper; the scarce asset is the **selection
function** — the operator's sense of what is good, currently exercised one
correction at a time. DotLn's bet is not that this delicate judgment can be
exhaustively formulated. It is that useful operational approximations can be
progressively arrived at: source incidents preserve what was felt, candidate
mechanisms approach it from different directions, and regression fixtures show
where each construction agrees or diverges. As mathematical or geometric
techniques can converge on a shape without becoming the shape itself, the
formulation is an instrument for approaching the operator's selection function,
not a claim to contain it precisely. **The model changes; the organization
survives.** Claude, Codex, a human, a shell script, and a future model are
interchangeable occupants of the same actor slot.

That bet needs an excellent foundation before it needs a long feature list. In
the reference implementation, the smallest useful loop—declare intent, see what
the system understood, observe authorized progress, receive timely feedback,
and inspect evidence—should already feel responsive, legible, and worth
repeating. Competitive gap-filling does not excuse a weak loop. When another
system introduces a useful idea, DotLn first asks whether the exact behavior can
be accommodated by existing primitives, compositions, ports, and runtime
lowerings. If not, the difference becomes evidence for one missing primitive or
boundary, not permission to bolt on an opaque special case. Integration and
semantic accommodation are preferred to imitation; both preserve every
capability contract the receiving implementation declares and expose any
omitted or lossy capability.

theses.title: The differentiated interface
theses.text:
## The differentiated interface

DotLn's second thesis is about _authoring_, not running:

> "I will take the entire Business, Leadership, and Personal Development shelf
> at Barnes & Noble and just map them to different agent / subagent
> communication structures... at once anyone who has read those books is an
> expert in some feature of the app — and it turns all those books into
> programming books overnight."

The analogies are not documentation — **the analogies are the ways you mix and
match the agents**. Every pattern (5S, the Ladder of Leadership, mitigated
speech, Theory of Constraints, commedia dell'arte roles, the
Algorithms-to-Live-By policies) compiles into exact mechanics, and the same
compiled program renders through an open-ended set of isomorphically equivalent
views: an RPG character with a Path-of-Exile-style socket-and-link build, a
business pattern card, a statechart, a function table, a marble/Morse temporal
track, a TypeScript DSL, an event timeline. Friendly metaphors are authoring
languages, never camouflage: every view either provably compiles to the same
normalized program or is labeled a lossy projection with the exact mechanics one
click away.

### Shape-first synthesis

The operator uses situations and analogies to communicate a desired **shape**: a
relationship, interaction, transition, contrast, feedback loop, or felt quality.
Literal similarity to the reference is not the acceptance test unless a specific
literal detail becomes load-bearing. Preserve the experience first, then
progressively lower it through observable interaction, domain mechanics,
contracts and evidence, and finally technology selected from representative
environment evidence. An imperfect analogy can carry a precise requirement;
source accidents do not become ontology by resemblance.

This is the standing interpretation rule for earlier and future operator
ideation. Its fullest product expression is the first-party application thesis,
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md), but it applies to the whole platform.

theses.title: Three horizons, one kernel
theses.text:
## Three horizons, one kernel

1. **Work operating system** — workstreams, disposable workers, evidence-backed
   completion, offline-capable state, a near-empty main thread. The immediate
   product.
2. **Executable pattern workshop** — the shelf-to-mechanism compiler and the
   drag-a-card-onto-an-agent authoring surface. The differentiated product.
3. **Agent ecology & simulation laboratory** — paired counterfactual runs,
   first-divergence detection, agent swaps, reflection-policy experiments over
   recorded event logs. The research product.

Horizon 3 must emerge from the same kernel (deterministic replay is what makes
counterfactuals possible at all) and is not allowed to distort Horizon 1.
The [workstream application candidate](12-workstream-application.md) develops
Horizon 1 through concrete end-user journeys and gradual workflow replacement,
including one outcome spanning multiple repositories. It leaves deployment and
application identity open and does not allocate another release rung.
[`προτείνω`](11-protino.md) is the operator-named application destination that
joins Horizons 2 and 3: prose-authored patterns and ad hoc interventions become
playable inside an inspectable counterfactual community. Naming the destination
does not move it ahead of the release ladder or make its application-local
content kernel doctrine.

theses.title: Mission — increase the chance of operator flow
theses.text:
## Mission — increase the chance of operator flow

This is the mission of the author's personal implementation and a motivating
use of the platform, not a compulsory objective or operating policy for every
DotLn owner.

AI-assisted work commonly falls into a babysitting mode: the operator repeatedly
restates context, supplies procedural guidance, coordinates tools and workers,
checks unsupported completion claims, recovers stalled work, and spends active
attention on the machinery instead of the idea. The desired alternative is not
unbounded improvisation or confidence without evidence. It is a sustained
creative flow in which the operator can keep the idea and implementation
direction in mind while the surrounding work behaves dependably.

The reference implementation's mission is to improve the conditions for that
**operator flow state**.
Supporting research, capability-building, coordination, routine procedure,
recovery, and verification should happen automatically when authorized,
predictably when routine, and helpfully when a genuinely material decision needs
the operator. Product and research investment should favor capabilities that
remove recurring supervision and avoidable context switches without exporting
their cost into correctness, authority, evidence, privacy, or recoverability.

The implementation cannot promise or infer a person's psychological state. It can
reduce interruption, repetition, manual ceremony, and rediscovery; preserve
intent and working context across handoffs; package necessary interruptions as
decision-ready inputs; and make recovery unsurprising. Under its selected
profile, flow does not silently authorize scope expansion, skipped verification,
perpetual action, or self-certification. “Give an agent a build, not your
biography” remains useful architectural shorthand for one mechanism serving
this larger mission.

exclusions.text:
Not an agent, an agent harness, or an agent-orchestration layer, as its
  identity. DotLn is an **agentic platform**: the shared substrate on which
  people and software actors hold work, authority, and evidence. It contains an
  orchestration layer and hosts harnesses as observed environments
  ([runtime primitive catalogs](03-architecture.md#runtime-primitive-catalogs)),
  but neither of those is what it is.
Not a prompt library, and not a wrapper that makes one vendor's model nicer.

Not a prescribed catalog of ideal agents, roles, personalities, workflows, or
  organizational doctrine. Bundled patterns are examples and optional starting
  points, not kernel truth.

Not dependent on a public marketplace. Local files, private catalogs,
  organization-internal registries, and offline or air-gapped installations
  remain complete authoring and distribution paths.

Not one prescribed autonomy curve. Presence and recorded time are policy
  inputs; an explicit owner policy may hold, shrink, grow, peak, reset, or loop
  scope and authority within its declared ceiling.

In the reference implementation, not a metrics theater: no invented numbers,
  no activity-as-progress, evidence precedes "done," and utilization is not the
  objective. A profile that omits verification says so instead.

The reference implementation is not finished when it works for its author:
  v1.0 means a person who has never read these docs can declare a bounded intent
  and receive a verifiable result.

orders.objective:
An instance's session finishes a starter update and a
release close without a step the kit did not run for it, the kit's admission
and prefix rules judge what they mean to judge, and the planner can ask for
the newest model:

- **The carried runtime is prepared where a build was tried.** In a kit
  root (`isKitRoot`), the emitted `recoverReleaseClose` runs the
  carried-runtime restore (`scripts/lib/release-kit-runtime.mjs`) and
  `harness emit` in place of `npm run build --silent`; `worktree finish`
  and `npm run harness` do the same; every advisory and refusal that tells
  an export to run `npm run build` names `node scripts/bootstrap.mjs` or the
  restore instead. In core nothing changes.
- **One command finishes the update.** `node scripts/launchpad.mjs update
  --finish` on a clean `main` fetches `origin`, fast-forwards `main` to
  `origin/main`, runs `bootstrapWorktree(root)` and prints what it did; it
  refuses, naming the fact, on a dirty tree, a non-fast-forward or a
  checkout that is not `main`. The README's route ends with it, and names
  that an explicit `--tags` fetch overrides `remote.upstream.tagOpt`.
- **The admission judges authority, not bytes.** The registered-target
  admission reads main's committed `dotln.config.json` and compares, between
  the worktree and main, only the registration's publication fields
  (`baseBranch`, `authorityProfile`, `release`, the roots) and the grants
  file, so an order that edits its own registration's gate commands is
  still admitted; any other difference in those fields withholds with the
  field named. A helper spelling that `plainShellWords` cannot parse but
  that begins with the admitted node spelling writes a `near-miss` advisory
  naming the shell syntax that hid it (a pipe, a redirect, a prefix), with
  no admission.
- **A prefix inside a paste is a prefix.** `recordOperatorMessage` finds the
  dispatch prefix at the start of the first non-blank line of the prompt
  after any fence or pasted-content framing the host adds, records which
  line held it, and still records one prefix per message.
- **The newest model on request.** `harness emit` writes
  `.claude/agents/dotln-worker-fable.md` (`model: claude-fable-5-1`,
  `effort: xhigh`) beside `dotln-worker`; the planner, refuter and reviewer
  role text admits it only when the operator's dispatch names it (the
  words `fable` or `fable 5.1` in the `planning:` or `resume:` line), the
  pinned worker stays the default, the direct refutation receipt and the
  response record which worker type ran, and product 07 §Model-specific
  notes states the opt-in.

orders.title: WO-227 — Outward publication reads as the operator intended: launchpad identifiers are refused in a target's commits and pull requests, the public word list and each private term are review items the reviewer confirms in context rather than bans on English words, an empty list is admitted, a generated Change-table path is named apart from the reviewed prose, the pull-request body keeps the meter block last behind a structural check, and a target's Release carries the reviewed notes when its order names them (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
An instance's reviewer publishes a target pull request, a
target Release and a launchpad pull request under checks that say what
they are for:

- **Identifiers never leave the launchpad.** A target's branch name,
  commit subjects, pull-request title and body carrying a launchpad
  identifier (`WO-NNN`, `WO-NNN-DNNN`, `FUP-<16 hex>`, `VER-NNN`,
  `FINAL-NNN`, `REVIEW-NNN`, `WS-NNN`) are refused naming the identifier
  and the rule; the kit's own records commit (its fixed message) and a
  `Closes #N` reference are not identifiers; a launchpad artifact keeps its
  convention (`# WO-NNN` titles).
- **Words are reviewed, not banned.** The public list (`reviewTerms`) and
  each private term marked `review` produce a `review` result that names
  the words (public) or the lines (private, never the term) and the
  section they sit in; the publish refuses until the reviewer passes
  `--confirm-terms sha256:<digest of the composed body>` after reading
  them, and the confirmation (digest, actor attestation, the count of
  matches) is recorded in the publication record and the journal. A
  private term marked `refuse` refuses as today. The English word alone
  never refuses anything.
- **Lists may be empty.** `reviewTerms: []` is a valid file, and a present
  local list with zero terms is `present` with a count of zero; an absent
  local list stays `unavailable` and refuses, as the floor requires.
- **Generated text is judged as generated text.** The Change table and the
  target-checks section are linted apart from the reviewed prose: an
  identifier or a `refuse` term in an added path refuses naming the path
  and the section; a review word in an added path joins the review list
  with its path; a path that already existed at the target's base is the
  target's own vocabulary and is not reported.
- **Planning warns early.** `plan check` lists, as an advisory, the paths a
  target order's Execution plan names that carry a review word or an
  identifier, so the order's author renames the file or lists the word
  deliberately before any draft publish.
- **The pull-request body has a shape.** `release prepare` and the
  regenerated body keep the meter block as the last block of the stored
  `PR.md`, after the prose, wherever it stood; `pullRequestBodyShapeFailures`
  refuses a stored body whose first non-blank line is not a level-one
  heading, that has no prose paragraph before the meter block or whose
  meter block is not last (the published body admits the product-gate
  block after it); it judges the current order's `PR.md` at publish and in
  `check-surfaces`, never a historical body; product 08 states the shape.
- **A target Release can carry the reviewed notes.** An order header
  `**Target release notes:** reviewed` makes the Release body the rendered
  five-section `RELEASE-NOTES.md` of that order at `sourceRevision` (the
  order title once under the overview, launchpad-relative links written as
  plain text or target-relative paths, the close line appended) and
  refuses, before any tag push, when the file is absent or fails

orders.title: WO-229 — A gate says who it waited for: each WAIT line labels its holders as this checkout, another checkout or unknown without printing a path, the gate summary and the recorded row carry the gate's lane wait apart from its work, the planning condition reports an execution-only median beside the wall-clock one and marks a contended sample, `node scripts/harness.mjs lanes` lists live holders read-only, and the structural tasks' full-capacity requests are measured against their need (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
When a gate waits, the operator can read who it waited for
and how long, in the terminal, in the recorded row and in the planning
condition, without any checkout's path leaving its machine; and the cause of
most cross-checkout waiting, the structural tasks' full-capacity requests,
is measured so the next pass can decide it:

- **WAIT names the relation.** Each holder in a WAIT line carries `this
  checkout`, `another checkout` or `checkout unknown` (a record without a
  `worktree` field), compared by `realpath` against the waiter's own
  worktree; the path is never printed.
- **The summary and the row carry the wait.** The gate summary line appends
  the gate's lane wait as the union of its tasks' wait intervals, split by
  relation (`; 1,512.3 s waiting for host lanes (1,512.3 s behind another
  checkout)`); the recorded check row gains `hostLaneWait: { wallMs,
  byRelation, holders: [{ task, slots, relation, nested }] }` with no path;
  `gateCriticalPath` splits `waitMs` into `laneWaitMs` and `gapMs`; gate
  reuse strips the new fields as it strips the old.
- **The planning condition tells the two apart.** The document-gate
  condition reports the wall-clock median as today and, beside it, an
  execution-only median (wall minus the recorded lane wait) read from each
  sample's recorded row, marks a sample that waited behind another checkout
  `contended`, and the host context carries a lane snapshot (holder count
  and slots by relation) in place of `other host activity unknown`; which
  figure `holds` judges is the decisions file's recorded choice (the
  planner proposes the execution-only figure for the cost condition and the
  wall figure for the operator's experience, both shown).
- **A read-only listing.** `node scripts/harness.mjs lanes` prints the live
  holders (relation, task, slots, age, nested, owner alive) and the recorded
  capacity through a non-mutating read, so an instance answers "is it me?"
  without reading JSON by hand or taking the lock.
- **The cause is measured, not assumed.** The executor measures, outside a
  gate, the CPU and RSS of each structural task and `kit-verify` in core and
  in a fixture export, and records in the decisions what a right-sized host
  request for each would be against the recorded capacity; if the
  measurement shows a task needing fewer than half the capacity, the
  request is sized to the measurement and the admission regression
  (criterion 5) proves a short document gate's wait is bounded while a
  complete gate runs; otherwise the order records the measurement and
  changes no request.

An operator at a launchpad, core or an exported instance,
runs the Entropy Reducer against a registered target repository or a
workstream's repositories with the discipline the launchpad review has:

- **The subject is a registered repository at a recorded commit.** `npm run
  entropy -- review --repository <id> [<commit>]` freezes a copy of the
  registered clone (`recordedRepositoryClone`, read in the order WO-223
  gives the moved-record reader) at the named commit, or at the clone's
  fetched base-branch head when none is named, exactly as the launchpad is
  frozen: a clone with no hard links and no checkout, detached at the
  commit, under the launchpad's scratch lane, with the dependency copy when
  the clone has one; the subject record's `repository` is the registration
  id, its hash covers it, and the receipt's subject names the repository,
  the commit and the frozen path. The pinned reviewer runs the same
  compiled program over that copy; the host revalidates the return; the
  receipt is filed and bound in the launchpad as today.
- **The refutation and the binding follow the subject.** `refute` freezes
  the same repository at the same commit for the blinded second worker; the
  filing's binding is the explicit-commit route (the named commit still
  resolves to the reviewed tree in the clone), the clone's refs and tracked
  status are witnessed before and after the episode and recorded, and the
  launchpad's own tracked status is recorded, not the subject.
- **Dispositions land in the launchpad's register and can target the
  workstream's orders.** `dispose … accept` appends the candidate under a
  heading that names the review, the repository and the commit, so the
  collector's row names the target and a planning pass allocates it with
  `--apply` to any order of the launchpad, the workstream's members
  included; proposal packets file under `docs/proposals/` as today.
- **A workstream is its member repositories.** `review --workstream WS-NNN` reads the distinct `repositoryId`s of the
  workstream document's `dotln-workstream` JSON block and dispatches the next
  member repository that has no filed review in the sequence (the launchpad
  itself when a member names `self`), returning as `review` does today; each
  receipt is filed by `entropy receipt` and carries the workstream id;
  `subject --workstream WS-NNN` names the next member to review, the pending
  dispatch or the receipt to consume, consuming before producing as today;
  each receipt's survivors are disposed in the pass (receipt 051).
- **The kit carries it.** The commands are kit files already; a kit fixture
  instance with a registered fixture target runs the subject and the review
  under the `fake` transport, and the review guide states the subjects.

orders.objective:
The source writer cannot damage the operator's repository,
and a writer's request reaches the operator. The writer's owned command
route and profile are removed by two independent, absence-tolerant
removals; a failed removal is a typed cleanup outcome naming the surviving
path; admission and after-tests refuse while any grant survives; settlement,
`WorkerInterrupted` and integrity are recorded before the cleanup's result
is judged; a restart removes the survivors and admits. Before the focused
after-tests the worktree is judged against the committed tree (a
`skip-worktree` or `assume-unchanged` entry, or a byte or mode differing
from the committed blob, refuses naming the path; nothing is restored), and
the verification worktree reads Git under the host's writer-resistant
argument set, so hidden modified, deleted and executable-bit files never
reach after-testing or publication and a planted configuration, replace ref
or commit graph cannot change what verification judges. The writer commits
on a detached worktree into a private object store, reading the shared
store through a read-only alternate with no write access to the shared
`objects`, `refs` or `logs`; after admission the host imports the
candidate's objects and only then creates the episode branch and updates
refs; the retained counterexample fails against the writer's access;
candidates still publish; a crash between import and ref update recovers
idempotently; concurrent `git gc` or `repack` neither loses data nor yields
an unjustified success. A writer that reports `status` other than
`completed`, or `requiresHuman`, ends its step `writer-requested-attention`
after the integrity and worktree checks, a rerun or restart keeps that end,
and the vertical records `NeedsHuman` with the request in its receipt. The
Codex writer's Git runs with rerere and automatic maintenance off, so its
`git commit -F` exits 0 under the `dotln-writer` grants while the shared Git
directory stays unwritable, requalified live at the installed Codex CLI on a
target with rerere enabled and packed refs, with denials read from the
host's own log. The Claude writer's launch environment carries the two
object-directory variables and the same two Git configuration pairs,
requalified live at the installed Claude CLI on a target with rerere
enabled: its commit lands in the private store, not the shared one, no
`rr-cache` and no maintenance write appears in the shared repository, and
the host imports and observes the commit. `dotln vertical` with a writer killed before commit exits 1
with a pending continuation, and a rerun completes the step with exactly one
commit. Ordinary recovery stays valid throughout.

criteria.text:
A profile already removed by an earlier partial cleanup leaves the route
   removed, the revocation recorded and nothing thrown (fixture).

With the profile's removal failing and then the route's, and with the
   route's failing and then the profile's, the other removal is attempted,
   each failure is recorded as `CommandCleanupFailed` naming the path, and
   admission and the focused after-tests refuse with a typed reason while
   the survivor exists; the records show settlement, `WorkerInterrupted`
   where the episode was interrupted, and the integrity result before the
   cleanup outcome (fixture, both orders, both writer accesses).

Under persistent removal failure the episode ends in the typed refusal
   naming the surviving path, never in a pass or an `observed` status
   (fixture).

After a restart, recovery removes the prior attempt's survivors and
   admits only when none survives (fixture).

No case of the cleanup matrix reaches an after-test or an admission while
   any grant survives (fixture assertion over every case).

A `skip-worktree` or `assume-unchanged` index entry on a modified,
   deleted or executable-bit-changed tracked file refuses before any focused
   after-test runs, with a typed reason naming the path; no candidate file
   is restored and no flag is cleared (fixture, each case).

A tracked file whose bytes or mode differ from the committed blob without
   any index flag refuses the same way; a clean candidate passes (fixture).

With a replace ref, a commit graph or a hooks path planted by the writer,
   the commit, tree and blob hashes the verification worktree judges equal
   those read in a clean clone with replace refs and the commit graph
   disabled; publication of such a candidate is refused when its real tree
   differs from the judged tree (fixture).

Ordinary recovery of an unreceipted prior attempt passes under the new
   check (fixture).

The D033 counterexample, committed as a case, fails at the base and
    passes at the repaired subject: the independent sibling blob survives
    the writer's deletion attempt, which is refused by the writer's access attempted inside the writer double's own process under the transport's
    emulated access (step 1), never from the host's `afterResult`,,
    and the episode does not report `observed`.

A writer's commits land in the private object store and not in the
    shared one; a write to the shared `objects/` directory from the writer
    is refused for both transports (confinement cases).

After admission the host imports the candidate's objects, verifies the
    imported tree equals the admitted tree and records `CandidateImported`
    before creating the episode branch or updating any ref; no shared ref
    names an object absent from the shared store at any point of the
    episode, including between the writer's commit and the import; an
    import whose tree differs is a typed stop naming the object and moves no
    ref; the candidate publishes as before.

A crash after import and before the ref update, and a crash before
    import, each recover with one ref update and no duplicate import record
    (fixture).

`git gc --prune=now` and `git repack -ad` on the shared store during an
    episode lose no object and produce no success without the
    re-verification passing (fixture).

With the Codex writer's launch environment, `git commit -F` in a linked
    worktree whose repository enables rerere and whose common directory is
    not writable exits 0, creates no `<common>/rr-cache` and starts no `git
    maintenance` child; with that environment's `GIT_CONFIG_*` pairs removed
    it exits 128 (fixture; fails before step 18; skipped only under uid 0).
    With the Claude writer's launch environment, the same commit in a
    linked worktree whose repository enables rerere and whose common
    directory is writable exits 0, creates no `<common>/rr-cache` and starts
    no `git maintenance` child (fixture; fails before step 18).

The Claude writer's launch environment carries `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY`,

    observes them live). The Codex writer's environment table carries `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY` and
    `GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES` beside `PATH` (the launch argument
    only; criterion 22 observes them in the writer's shell) and
    `rerere.enabled=false` and `maintenance.auto=false` through
    `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`; no `dotln-writer` grant names the common directory,
    `packed-refs`, `packed-refs.lock` or `rr-cache`; the grant set step 13
    pins (the private store in place of the shared `objects`, `refs` and
    `logs`), `network.enabled=false`, `PATH` and the Claude `--allowedTools`

For both transports, a writer that reports `blocked`, `failed` or

    the integrity check and before any effect read, observed-commit check,
    after-test, receipt, `CandidateImported` or episode branch; a rerun

Through `runVerticalIssue`, a source writer reporting `blocked` with

`dotln vertical` with the fixture writer killed before commit exits 1

    `WorkerInterrupted` reason `interrupted` and no signal; a rerun exits 0

The vertical's recovery probe passes at the repaired subject, and both
    transports' confinement cases pass.

The Codex probe's `sandbox` record, at the installed Codex CLI and under the

    `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY` and `GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES` into the
    writer's shell (the writer holds no write access to the shared objects);
    the calibrated reader over the writer's process window

The Claude probe's record, within at most two episodes (a second only

    the episode's private store and absent from the shared store read
    without alternates, which is this order's live observation that the
    installed Claude CLI passed `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY` and
    `GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES` to the writer's `git commit`; at the

    and no maintenance write appear in the shared repository: against the
    snapshot taken at `SourceChangeProcessStarted`, no `<common>/rr-cache`

    own worktree administrative directory (and its private store, if that

    observation that the CLI also passed the Git
    configuration pairs; the host then records `CandidateImported` and
    `SourceChangeObserved`; the record carries the CLI version, model,
    effort, wall-clock and token usage, and no home-directory path.

Write-backs land as step 33 lists them, each in place with no dated
    paragraph: product 03 §Session lifecycle & resilience (the settlement
    order with the surviving-grant refusal and the writer's object authority,
    a private store and a host-owned import after admission, replacing the
    narrowed shared-state sentence; no sentence count binds it) and §Ports (the clause, the Codex writer sentence, the Claude writer
    clause and the writer-request sentence); the skeleton README sentence;
    the decisions file with every record step 33 names; FUP-6c444dbf9a4d92bb
    disposed onto the Codex qualification's decision and
    FUP-42ef16541a8893b9 onto the Claude requalification's; the

    the publication locks refreshed. No byte figure binds these write-backs.

`npm test -- --review` and `npm run test:docs` green; `git diff --check`

orders.title: WO-192 — One session drives an order through its whole lifecycle: a router that only routes starts a fresh worker for each phase and hands it nothing but the phrase, for the launchpad's own orders and for a registered target's, whose phase workers run in the target worktree under WO-049's bundle (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
The operator types one phrase naming an order and one
session carries it from its current phase to a pull request ready to
merge, then, typed again after the merge, through release close. That
session only routes: every phase is done by a fresh worker that
received the phrase and nothing else, runs its own dispatch, keeps its
own sub-agent budget and records its own completion. The order may be the
launchpad's own or a registered target's (WO-071, WO-072): for a target
order each phase's worker runs in the target worktree WO-072 created,
governed by the bundle WO-049 emitted there, and is launched from the
instance, so the operator never opens a session in a target repository.

reviewer, release-close) at the pinned model and effort, from the generator and check rule WO-187 adds for spawned workers
(`packages/compiler/src/harness.ts`), a session record, role and

orders.title: WO-207 — Instance update control: an instance takes kit machinery with its build pinned or followed, keeps its own code at a manifest-excluded extension root that the kit's machinery loads through the SourceAdapter port and no update touches, rolls back its last update to the prior kit state, and takes a starter update only through an upgrade order its own planning pass cuts, gated by kit conformance and its own declared suites (version assigned at activation)
orders.objective:
An instance controls the kit updates it takes, from core and
inside the instance:

- **Its own code.** `dotln.config.json` may declare `extensions`: a root
  outside every kit tree (default `extensions/`) and adapters by kind
  (`source`, `effect`, `projection`). A vertical issue naming
  `source: "<id>"` has `prepare()` load that adapter, record
  `ExtensionLoaded { id, kind, path, sha256 }` and call its `fetchBundle`
  in place of `fetchIssueBundle`, with the bundle passing the same checks
  as the GitHub source's; `effect` and `projection` adapters are admitted
  and listed, never imported here. No export, manifest or update touches
  the root; the README states the review burden. The first consumer is a
  fixture adapter; the enterprise-tracker adapter is the work instance's.
- **Its build.** The kit manifest names its build (the compiled definition
  modules, their semantic hash and compiler version). An update takes
  `both` (today's), `machinery` (build modules kept at their pinned bytes,
  `build.pin` recorded, emit, check and `kit-verify` honoring it) or `build`
  (the build alone, then the re-emit), and refuses an incompatible pairing
  before any write; inside an instance, the upgrade order runs
  `build --pin` or `build --take` after its merge, as the channel the
  operator chose. WO-076's overlay composes over whichever build is pinned.
- **Its way back.** Each update logs what it did and keeps retained copies,
  refusing before any write when it cannot. `rollback` inside the instance,
  or `export --update <dir> --rollback` from core, returns the kit files
  and manifest to the logged state before the last update, reverses the
  reversible instance actions (the update's `build.pin` among them), lists
  the rest by id, logs itself and prints the re-emit, which the role that
  ran it runs next; it refuses, naming the path or row, after a later kit
  edit, when the update is not the latest, or when a prior file has no
  verified source.
- **Its way in.** An instance takes a starter update through the session-run
  route the client README records since WO-210: the incoming revision
  previewed from a detached worktree of that revision, the merge on an update
  branch, the re-emit and lineage index, one commit, the push and the update
  pull request the operator merges (the personal fork took its #1, #3, #8 and
  #16 this way). For the operator's instances the upgrade order a planning
  pass (dedicated, or part of one) cuts from the kit's template is that
  route's recorded form: it names the starter revision, the channel and each
  refused path's resolution, carries the route as its plan, runs the channel's
  `build` form after the merge and passes the gate below; the template's
  rollback form takes the way back the same way. A planning branch writes only
  `docs/` and root Markdown (WO-135), so the pass never applies kit files.
- **Its gate.** The consumer selection WO-213 decided (WO-213-D014: the six
  structural tasks and `kit-verify`, run fresh; carried kit suites stay
  explicit `--only` and `--machinery` diagnostics) plus the instance's own
  additions, the planner's proposal (assumption 8): suites it declares in
  `dotln.config.json` `suites` (name, command and sources), selected by
  changed sources, appended to that selection and run fresh, with each
  extension adapter naming the suite that covers it. Core's own gate is
  unchanged.
- **No step is the operator's by hand.** The operator gives the word (the
  starter revision, the channel, how each refused path resolves, a
  rollback), types the dispatch phrases and merges the pull request; a
  role runs every command and makes every commit (operator direction,
  2026-10-13; planning document §12.1).

In an exported fixture instance, `parity init` writes the rows file from
   the seed at the configured path and creates the ignored registry, a
   second `init` changes no byte, and the kit manifest lists the command,
   the templates, the schema and the seed and neither the rows file nor the
   registry; `git status` shows no tracked change from `init`.

`parity add` writes a row and refuses one whose fields do not fit its
   status, naming the field as `PARITY_FIELD_<NAME>`; a table test covers
   every status.

`parity check` refuses, naming the row: a carrier absent from a fixture
   build and order set; a `unit` or `support` carrier under a fixture
   `build: none` manifest, naming the build; a `lossy` row that says
   nothing is lost; an `unmapped` row with neither a request nor a
   decision; and a private field's text found in a kit file or a request
   draft.

`parity report` over a synthetic set of two generations prints the
   counts and, per generation, whether it is at least as capable, with the
   rows that prevent it.

`parity request <row>` writes a request draft whose body is the row's
   generic statement; a test shows that no other field of the row appears
   in the draft.

An update fixture leaves the rows file and the registry byte for byte
   unchanged, and an export from a core checkout that holds a synthetic
   rows file writes none of it into the kit.

Every row, fixture and example committed by this order is synthetic or
   quoted from product 12 or the critical path document, each seed
   `source.quote` a substring of its `document`; the final review records
   the check that found it so. The write-backs of step 7 state, in product
   12, where an instance keeps this private state and the report as an
   instance's parity measure, in product 10 the mapping statuses in use by
   the instance map, and in the client README the command; `npm run meta
   -- --check` passes.

The re-mints of step 6 are recorded; `npm test -- --review` and `npm
   run test:docs` green; `git diff --check` clean; no new dependency. No

## Goal-aligned decisions

The Contributor's purpose comes from [the vision](00-vision.md): DotLn is a
local-first, model-agnostic compiler/runtime for human judgment. This personal
implementation aims to improve operator flow by moving recurring supervision,
coordination, recovery and verification into dependable machinery, while
preserving correctness, authority, evidence, privacy and recoverability.

The current [critical-path plan](../planning/critical-path-2026-09-08.md) targets
the always-on runtime, its first real external source change and an independently
verified source-to-deliverable loop.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

**Platform lens.** Four checks from the platforms lesson the operator
pointed at (Steve Yegge's 2011 account of the Amazon service mandate) apply
to any capability a plan or order lands: it arrives as an interface
something else consumes (a transport profile, a typed event, a projection, a
handoff packet), never only as a script or a session; it is externalizable
by construction (content-addressed inputs, declared contracts, no private
setting as the source of a guarantee); this repository and the operator's
own repository consume it before any export; and its result is usable by a
stranger to the session, so a receipt that needs reverse-engineering is an
accessibility failure [[vision-into-use pass](../planning/vision-into-use-2026-09-17.md)
§12, 2026-09-17]. The planning refuter's platform-first standard is
unchanged.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:start -->

Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.

<!-- dotln-goal-rules:end -->

The shared supports carry these duties and their compiled identity in both
harnesses. They are instruction-level judgment, not proof that an agent applied
every lens or a causal detector. The meter's five quantitative trap signals are
separate. General Naive Interventionism, NoOp and adaptive Tinkerer mechanics
retain their candidate scope; this bounded Contributor policy does not claim
their generalized implementations. The [WO-043 receipt](../evidence/WO-043/ideation-commands-and-usage.md)
records this promotion and its limits.

episode.statement: I judged the 2026-10-21 fork-notes planning pass (scope "pass": all 19 sequenced orders, WO-226 to WO-228) as the independent plan refuter. Mask Contra-Auguste, lens architecture-and-semantics. I worked against the compiled subject in docs/control/local/refute-prompt-2026-10-21-fork-notes.json at faa1945f. Verdict: aligned-with-findings, with no holds. Five orders are aligned (WO-204, WO-183, WO-091, WO-096, and one more counted in the 19 with no findings is none; precisely WO-204, WO-183, WO-091 and WO-096). Fifteen are aligned-with-findings, with 22 known-issue findings in total. I found no observed failure against the five cost-table trap observations and no contradiction of a supplied vision passage, so nothing rose to misaligned. The main findings: WO-227 makes unmarked private terms review-by-default, so a reviewer, not the operator, can confirm a private-term match. WO-226's admission change lets an order alter its own target-gate commands. WO-226 and WO-192 add role text against 281 and 424 bytes of reviewer and executor cold-start headroom, while the cost table shows eleven 4 KB ceiling raises. WO-220 and WO-204 each owe a live feedback episode on the same source-change-host.ts. WO-207's starter-refresh admission of the update-log row has no criterion. WO-193's Cost line cites a criterion 14 that no longer exists and keeps merge savings that the WO-228 split undid. sequence.md calls WO-228 'blocked by nothing' although its criterion 5 needs WO-193's draftRequest. WO-224 sits before the critical-path run without being its prerequisite. WO-083, WO-014 and WO-088 can close criteria by waiver or unmet-by-design. How I worked: 66 tool calls, 65 Bash and 1 Read of my own persisted tool output; none spawned an agent. One Bash call tried to write a copy of the cost table to the session scratchpad; the project hook refused it as an outside-project write and nothing was written. Two other calls ended non-zero: a zsh quoting error and an intentional validator smoke test. I made no repository or Git writes. I read the whole prompt JSON (all subject sections, all 19 orders' objective, cost, criteria and non-goals) and docs/planning/sequence.md in full. To check cited claims, I read targeted excerpts or greps of these order files: WO-192, WO-193, WO-207, WO-219, WO-220, WO-225, WO-226 and WO-227. Those excerpts included a few lines naming earlier receipts 045, 049 and 050 that the 2026-10-21 pass wrote into the orders; I opened no receipt files. I also read docs/control/budgets.json and excerpts of docs/product/07-execution-guide.md and docs/product/02-domain-model.md. I read scripts/lib/terms.mjs (head) and greps or excerpts of these: packages/compiler/src/harness.ts, scripts/lib/target-gate.mjs, scripts/lib/starter-refresh.mjs, scripts/lib/evidence-sources.mjs, packages/skeleton/src/feedback-audit.ts, packages/skeleton/src/runtime-inputs.mjs, scripts/release.mjs, scripts/test-runner.mjs, scripts/lib/plan-direct.mjs and packages/skeleton/src/plan-refutation-protocol.ts. I did not open any other docs/planning file, docs/intake or refutation receipts. I validated the result by piping it on stdin to the repository's own validatePlanResult (packages/skeleton/dist/src/plan-refutation-protocol.js) with the prompt's subject. It returned the identical object: planVerdict aligned-with-findings and 0 holds. Model: claude-opus-5-5, as stated by the host system prompt. Effort: the shell environment reads CLAUDE_EFFORT=xhigh, which may be inherited from the parent session; I had no per-agent effort readback.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate S (the starter's updates reach an instance) feeding gate P: WO-083's activation preflight requires the instance's main to carry a starter merge taken by the instance's update route, and this order makes that route and the following release close finish in an export without a hand step. It is not a hard prerequisite: sequence.md records that the fork proceeds with nothing waiting on core and calls these items workarounds. NoOp cost in the records: the cost table's WO-226 row has metrics null (unstarted), so no measured cost exists; the Cost line names seven observed fork states of 2026-10-21 that persist under NoOp: a release close withheld on ENOENT tsconfig.json in an export, a bootstrap the session must remember after each update, three texts telling an export to run a build it cannot run, an admission withheld because an order edited its own registration, a piped helper spelling that left no row and no advisory, a pasted dispatch prefix that left a whole planning pass without its role, and no operator-selectable Fable worker. Checked at faa1945f: the emitted recoverReleaseClose runs npm run build --silent (packages/compiler/src/harness.ts, releaseCloseRecovery) and isKitRoot exists (packages/skeleton/src/runtime-inputs.mjs). The fork took updates #1, #3, #8 and #16 by the session-run route, so the hand step recurs per update.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the admission relaxation and the near-miss advisory reduce refusals rather than add one; the policy-resistance observation already falls 9, 6, 2, 0, 0. Tragedy of the commons: the carried-runtime restore stays inside the recovery's 120 s child bound and the Fable worker is opt-in, but one sentence of role text enters the planner, refuter and reviewer roots while the drift-to-low-performance observation puts the reviewer root at 28,603 of 28,884 bytes (281 bytes of headroom) and the Cost line states no cold-start figure (finding). Drift to low performance: the standing route answers a breached ceiling with a one-step 4 KB raise (eleven cold-start acceptances in the cost table), so an unaccounted sentence normalizes a larger cold start. Escalation: seven unrelated bullets in one order (14 steps, about 30 KB) widen verification while five of the last eight first verifications failed (cost table firstVerifications). Success to the successful: a Git hook and a SessionStart preparation are named non-goals, so alternatives were weighed. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: removes recurring operator rescue (remembering bootstrap, re-dispatching a pass whose prefix was lost). Rule beating: the Fable admission is role text only, so a green harness check and the sentence's presence pass without anything preventing an undispatched Fable spawn, and the admission relaxation lets an order change the commands its own target gate runs (findings). Seeking the wrong goal: six bullets serve operator flow in the instance; the Fable bullet answers an operator question and unblocks no gate.
orders.removalBalance: Yes for six of seven parts: the additions are one-time source edits (about ten files, six test files, 14 steps, one compiler minor with deterministic re-mints, no live feedback episode) and the removals are recurring per update and per release close in every export (a failed close, a remembered bootstrap, misleading build advice, a withheld admission, a lost dispatch role). The Fable part names no removal beyond 'a worker model the operator cannot select' while adding a second generated agent definition, role text in three roots and a workerType field in the refutation receipt, so for that part the addition is larger than the removal.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades: in core nothing changes; update --finish refuses before any write on a dirty tree, a non-fast-forward or a non-main checkout, leaving the existing manual route intact; a near-miss spelling yields an advisory, never an admission or a refusal; a prompt with no prefix stays unclassified as today; the pinned worker stays the default. Two parts change behavior instead of degrading: the admission now admits a differing dotln.config.json outside the publication fields (a relaxation of an authority check), and the first-line rule reads a prefix after a leading fence, so quoted content whose first line begins with a dispatch prefix becomes a dispatch (findings).
